evidenceAudit.scope: Acute asthma attacks in children aged 1 year and over in India: severity, oxygen, salbutamol by spacer or nebuliser, ipratropium, oral prednisolone, IV magnesium and second-line IV treatment, admission and discharge, using BTS/SIGN 158 (2019) and a SIGN 158-referenced hospital protocol because no Indian paediatric acute asthma guideline with doses could be opened. The adult Acute severe asthma (India) topic covers adults.
findings: Oxygen to SpO2 94–98%, salbutamol pMDI and spacer 1 puff every 30–60 seconds up to 10 puffs, nebulised salbutamol 2.5–5 mg every 20–30 minutes for SpO2 below 92%, ipratropium 250 micrograms, prednisolone by age (10 mg under 2, 20 mg 2–5 years, 30–40 mg over 5 years) for up to 3 days, IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg, nebulised magnesium 150 mg, no routine antibiotics checked against SIGN 158 (Right Decision Service).

IV magnesium 40 mg/kg (maximum 2 g), IV salbutamol 15 micrograms/kg, aminophylline 5 mg/kg then infusion, severity bands and discharge criteria checked against the NHS Borders SIGN 158-referenced protocol (2020).

Management sequence reformatted on 2026-10-26: first step is an ABCDE survey where the topic is acute; every drug mention is a medication badge (drug, dose, route, frequency, duration) copied from this topic's medicine table; side-effect, contraindication and dose-adjustment wording was removed from the sequence (it stays in the medicine table). No other clinical content was changed.

[SUPPLEMENTED - EXTERNAL] ABCDE first-step doses (oxygen, 0.9% sodium chloride bolus, 10% glucose) are standard resuscitation doses from Resuscitation Council UK ABCDE approach (2021) for adults and APLS 6th edition (2016) for children; they were not taken from this topic's cited sources.

IV magnesium infusion duration is not stated in the opened protocol (usually over 20 minutes).
Heart and respiratory rate thresholds by age are not in the opened sources.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute asthma is a common cause of paediatric emergency visits in India, often triggered by viral infections, smoke from biomass fuels, dust and seasonal changes. Airway inflammation, bronchospasm and mucus narrow the airways, causing wheeze, breathlessness and hypoxaemia; a silent chest and exhaustion signal a life-threatening attack. Early inhaled salbutamol, ideally by metered-dose inhaler and spacer, and early oral steroid reduce admissions. Severe attacks need oxygen, nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium, and IV magnesium or other second-line drugs if there is no response (SIGN 158). Children with frequent attacks often have under-treated persistent asthma, poor inhaler technique or no preventer, so every acute visit is a chance to check technique, start or step up an inhaled steroid, and reduce smoke exposure at home.
keyMechanisms: Allergen, viral or irritant triggers cause airway inflammation and smooth-muscle contraction.
Narrowed airways cause air trapping and ventilation-perfusion mismatch.
Fatigue and rising PaCO2 signal impending respiratory failure.
Beta-2 agonists relax airway smooth muscle; steroids reduce inflammation.

symptoms: Night-time or exercise-induced cough and wheeze before the attack (poor control)
physicalSigns: SpO2 below 92% in air (severe, SIGN 158); give oxygen if below 94%
Silent chest or markedly reduced air entry (severe)
redFlags: Silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, exhaustion (SIGN 158)
precipitants: Smoke from biomass fuel or tobacco

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Infant under 1 year with coryza, crackles and wheeze and poor bronchodilator response; clinical diagnosis by age and course.
Fever, focal crackles or bronchial breathing and tachypnoea out of proportion to wheeze; chest X-ray consolidation settles it.
Sudden choking onset, unilateral wheeze or reduced air entry; chest X-ray air trapping and bronchoscopy settle it.
Barking cough and inspiratory stridor rather than expiratory wheeze; clinical diagnosis responds to steroid.
Wheeze with urticaria, angioedema or hypotension after a trigger; clinical diagnosis — give IM adrenaline.
Sudden worsening with unilateral reduced breath sounds and hyper-resonance during an attack; chest X-ray settles it.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: SpO2 above 94%; PEF above 80% predicted; not distressed.
SpO2 91–95%; PEF 50–80%; distressed with obvious accessory muscle use.
SpO2 below 92%; PEF below 50%; marked distress, silent chest, pulsus paradoxus.

clinicalManagement.title: ABCDE survey with concurrent correction
actions: Work through Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability and Exposure in order, and correct each abnormality concurrently as it is found: do not wait for the full survey, investigations or a diagnosis before treating a life-threatening problem, and call for senior help early.

Airway: look, listen and feel for obstruction; open it with a neutral head position (head tilt in older children) or jaw thrust, suction secretions, use an oropharyngeal airway if unconscious and call for expert paediatric airway help if it cannot be kept patent.

Breathing: count respiratory rate, measure SpO2, check recession, grunting, nasal flaring and air entry; if SpO2 is below 94% give [💊 Oxygen | 10–15 L/min via reservoir mask | Inhaled | Continuous | Until SpO2 94–98%, then titrate to target] and treat life-threatening chest problems as they are found.

Circulation: check heart rate, capillary refill and blood pressure, attach a monitor and secure IV access if the attack is severe; if shocked give [💊 Sodium chloride 0.9% | 10 mL/kg | IV or IO bolus over 10 minutes | Reassess after each bolus; repeat if still shocked | Until perfusion restored].

Disability: assess responsiveness (alert, voice, pain, unresponsive), pupils and posture, and measure capillary glucose; if glucose is below 3 mmol/L give [💊 Glucose 10% | 2 mL/kg | IV or IO bolus | Repeat after 10 minutes if glucose remains below 3 mmol/L | Until glucose 3 mmol/L or above]; look for seizure activity.
Exposure: expose the child to examine fully while preventing heat loss; check temperature, skin (rash, bruising, wounds) and abdomen, then cover again.

clinicalManagement.title: Start treatment
actions: Give [💊 Oxygen | 10–15 L/min via reservoir mask | Inhaled | Continuous | Until SpO2 94–98%, then titrate to target] if SpO2 is below 94% (SIGN 158).

Give [💊 Salbutamol | 1 puff (100 micrograms) every 30–60 seconds, up to 10 puffs | Inhaled via pMDI and spacer (face mask under 3 years) | Repeat every 20–30 minutes as needed | Until improved, then 3–4-hourly]; if SpO2 is below 92% use [💊 Salbutamol | under 5 years 2.5 mg; 5 years and over 5 mg | Nebulised, oxygen-driven | Every 20–30 minutes | Until improved] (SIGN 158).
Give early [💊 Prednisolone | under 2 years 10 mg; 2–5 years 20 mg; over 5 years 30–40 mg | Oral | Once daily | Up to 3 days] (SIGN 158).

clinicalManagement.title: Severe or not responding
actions: Repeat [💊 Salbutamol | under 5 years 2.5 mg; 5 years and over 5 mg | Nebulised, oxygen-driven | Every 20–30 minutes | Until improved] and add [💊 Ipratropium bromide | 250 micrograms (125 micrograms under 1 year; 500 micrograms 12 years and over) | Nebulised with salbutamol | Every 20–30 minutes in the first hours, then 4–6-hourly | Until improved] (SIGN 158).
Consider [💊 Magnesium sulfate nebulised | 150 mg | Nebulised with each salbutamol dose | With each dose in the first hour | First hour only] if SpO2 is below 92% (SIGN 158).
If still not responding give [💊 Magnesium sulfate | 40 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) | IV infusion | Once | Single dose] (BGH/SIGN 158).

clinicalManagement.title: Second-line IV
actions: Under senior and paediatric intensive care unit input give [💊 Salbutamol | over 2 years 15 micrograms/kg over 10 minutes (1 month–2 years 5 micrograms/kg over 5 minutes); then infusion 60–300 micrograms/kg/hour | IV | Bolus, then infusion | Until improved] or [💊 Aminophylline | 5 mg/kg (maximum 500 mg) over at least 20 minutes, then 1 mg/kg/hour (1 month–12 years) or 500–700 micrograms/kg/hour (over 12 years) | IV | Loading, then infusion | Until improved] (BGH/SIGN 158).
Rising PaCO2, exhaustion or falling consciousness: call anaesthesia and PICU for airway support (BGH/SIGN 158).

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge
actions: Stable on 3–4-hourly bronchodilator, PEF above 75%, SpO2 above 94% in air (BGH/SIGN 158).
Personalised action plan; review within 48 hours (BGH/SIGN 158).

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent the next attack
actions: Check inhaler and spacer technique; start or step up an inhaled corticosteroid preventer if attacks are frequent (SIGN 158, discharge and follow-up; see the Asthma: long-term care topic for preventer doses).
Advise avoiding tobacco and biomass smoke; give a written action plan and review within 48 hours (BGH/SIGN 158).

vignette.text: Meera, a 7-year-old girl from Lucknow weighing 22 kg, is brought in November with 2 days of cough and increasing wheeze after a cold. She lives in a household that cooks with wood. She can speak only a few words at a time, uses her neck muscles to breathe and has an SpO2 of 90% in air. Respiratory rate is 40/min, pulse 140/min, and peak flow is 40% of predicted. She uses a salbutamol inhaler without a spacer.

guidedApproach.title: Inflammation, spasm and air trapping
guidedApproach.prompt: Why does an acute attack become dangerous?
guidedApproach.guidance: Viral infection, smoke or allergen exposure triggers airway inflammation with mucosal oedema, mucus plugging and smooth-muscle contraction. Narrowed airways close early in expiration, trapping air and flattening the diaphragm, which increases the work of breathing. Uneven ventilation causes hypoxaemia. Early in an attack the child hyperventilates and PaCO2 falls; a normal or rising PaCO2 means fatigue and impending respiratory failure. A silent chest means so little air moves that wheeze cannot be heard. Beta-2 agonists relax smooth muscle within minutes, anticholinergics add bronchodilation in severe attacks, and steroids reduce inflammation over hours.

guidedApproach.title: Grade the attack in seconds
guidedApproach.prompt: Which signs define a severe or life-threatening attack?
guidedApproach.guidance: Assess speech, work of breathing, air entry, SpO2, heart and respiratory rate, and peak flow in children aged 5 and over. A moderate attack has SpO2 of 92% or more (BGH bands moderate as 91–95%, which overlap), PEF 50–80% and the child can talk. A severe attack has SpO2 below 92%, PEF below 50%, inability to complete sentences or feed, and marked accessory muscle use. Life-threatening features are a silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, exhaustion, confusion or drowsiness, and hypotension. Consider other diagnoses in infants under 2 years with poor response, and look for pneumothorax if a child suddenly worsens.

guidedApproach.title: Few tests, used wisely
guidedApproach.prompt: When are tests useful in acute asthma?
guidedApproach.guidance: Pulse oximetry guides oxygen and severity, and peak flow in children aged 5 and over measures response and the discharge threshold of 75% or more. Most children need no blood tests or X-ray. Take a blood gas when the attack is severe or not improving: a PaCO2 above 6 kPa is a danger sign. A chest X-ray is reserved for severe or non-responding asthma, focal signs or suspected pneumothorax, collapse or consolidation. Check potassium when salbutamol is given repeatedly or intravenously, because beta-2 agonists drive potassium into cells.

guidedApproach.title: Bronchodilate early, add steroid, escalate on time
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you treat acute asthma step by step?
guidedApproach.guidance: Give oxygen to keep SpO2 94–98%. For mild to moderate attacks give salbutamol by metered-dose inhaler and spacer, 1 puff every 30–60 seconds up to 10 puffs, repeated every 20–30 minutes; a spacer works as well as a nebuliser. Nebulise salbutamol (2.5 mg under 5 years, 5 mg from 5 years) with ipratropium 250 micrograms when SpO2 is below 92%. Give prednisolone early: 10 mg under 2 years, 20 mg at 2–5 years, 30–40 mg over 5 years, for up to 3 days. If there is no response, give IV magnesium 40 mg/kg (maximum 2 g), then IV salbutamol or aminophylline with PICU input.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 7-year-old girl has an asthma attack after a cold. She can say only a few words, SpO2 is 90% in air, respiratory rate 40/min and peak flow 40% of predicted. She has not yet had any treatment in the emergency department.
boardQuestions.question: What is the best initial treatment?

options.explanation: Oral salbutamol acts slowly and is not used for acute attacks.

options.text: Oxygen, nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 250 micrograms, and oral prednisolone 30–40 mg
options.explanation: Correct. SpO2 below 92% and PEF below 50% mean a severe attack needing oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators and early steroid (SIGN 158).
Aminophylline is second-line after inhaled therapy and magnesium fail.
Antibiotics are not routinely given in acute asthma.
Treatment must not wait; X-ray is only for selected children.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: SpO2 below 92%: oxygen, nebulised salbutamol plus ipratropium, prednisolone.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 5-year-old boy with a severe asthma attack has received three nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium doses and oral prednisolone over an hour. He is still working hard to breathe with SpO2 91% on oxygen and poor air entry. He weighs 18 kg and is alert.
boardQuestions.question: What is the next step?

options.explanation: He has already received steroid, and a second dose adds no immediate effect.
He is still severely unwell and needs escalation.
Sedatives can depress breathing and are dangerous in acute asthma.

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate 40 mg/kg (720 mg) over 20 minutes
options.explanation: Correct. IV magnesium is the next step when severe asthma does not respond to inhaled therapy (BGH/SIGN 158).
There is no sign of bacterial infection and antibiotics will not relieve bronchospasm.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: No response after an hour: IV magnesium 40 mg/kg.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 9-year-old girl has had three emergency visits for asthma this year. Today's attack has settled with salbutamol by spacer and prednisolone. Her peak flow is now 85% of predicted and SpO2 97% in air. She uses only a salbutamol inhaler without a spacer, and her family cooks with wood indoors.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most important addition to her discharge plan?

options.explanation: A spacer works as well as a nebuliser and is cheaper and quicker.
Long-term oral steroids are not appropriate for this level of asthma.

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroid preventer with a spacer, smoke reduction and a written action plan
options.explanation: Correct. Frequent attacks indicate a need for preventer therapy, good technique and trigger reduction (SIGN 158, discharge and follow-up).
Antibiotics treat bacterial infection and do not prevent asthma attacks.
Exercise should be encouraged once asthma is controlled.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: Every attack is a chance to start a preventer and fix technique.

patientEducation: Spacer technique and written action plan.
Use preventer inhaler daily as prescribed.
Return if reliever needed more than 4-hourly.
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid smoke from tobacco and biomass fuels.
dischargeCriteria: PEF above 75% predicted or best; SpO2 above 94% in air (BGH)

nodes.text: Child with acute wheeze and breathlessness
Life-threatening: silent chest, cyanosis, poor effort, exhaustion, confusion or hypotension?
Senior and PICU now: oxygen, back-to-back nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium, prednisolone or IV hydrocortisone, early IV magnesium 40 mg/kg, consider IV salbutamol
Severe: SpO2 below 92%, PEF below 50%, cannot complete sentences, marked accessory muscle use?
Oxygen to 94–98%; nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium every 20–30 minutes; prednisolone; consider nebulised magnesium
Admit; space salbutamol as tolerated; continue prednisolone
Still not responding or rising PaCO2?
Senior and PICU: IV salbutamol or aminophylline; prepare for airway support
Admit; close monitoring and potassium checks
Oxygen if SpO2 below 94%; salbutamol by spacer, 1 puff every 30–60 seconds up to 10 puffs; prednisolone
Discharge with action plan, preventer review and follow-up in 48 hours
Treat as severe: nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium; admit
